# rigid-dynamics.library: SolvePositionRow

**Tier:** `future`. **File:** [rigid-dynamics.library](../rigid-dynamics.library.md). **Source:** [stdlib/future/rigid-dynamics.library.plato, line 774](../../../../../stdlib/future/rigid-dynamics.library.plato#L774).

This slice: SolvePositionRow, SolvePositionPass, SolvePositions, ApplyGravityAndDamping, IntegratePoses, Step, StepMany, StepBallScene, Earth, SixtyHertz.

```plato

    // The world after solving row `index` once for POSITION: the normal axis only,
    // aiming at the correction speed, with no restitution and no friction. Friction
    // is deliberately absent — a fictitious tangential velocity would shear a stack
    // sideways as it settles.
    //
    // The row's NormalImpulse field is reused as the accumulator for the pseudo
    // impulse, so the clamp is on the accumulated value exactly as in the velocity
    // solve and a later row can undo an earlier row's over-push. That reuse is safe
    // because `SolvePositions` runs on a copy whose constraints it discards; only
    // the body twists survive.
    SolvePositionRow(world: RigidWorld3D, index: Integer): RigidWorld3D
    {
        var row = world.Constraints[index];
        var a = world.Bodies[row.BodyA.Value];
        var b = world.Bodies[row.BodyB.Value];
        var n = row.Normal.Vector;
        var increment = ImpulseFor(
            CorrectionSpeed(row.Penetration, world.Solver, world.TimeStep.FixedDeltaTime.Seconds),
            SeparationSpeed(a, b, row.Point, n),
            DirectionalMass(a, b, row.Point, n));
        var total = (row.NormalImpulse.Amount + increment).Max(0.0);
        var applied = total - row.NormalImpulse.Amount;
        return RigidWorld3D(
            ReplacedAt(
                ReplacedAt(world.Bodies, row.BodyA.Value, ApplyImpulse(a, n * -applied, row.Point)),
                row.BodyB.Value,
                ApplyImpulse(b, n * applied, row.Point)),
            ReplacedAt(world.Constraints, index, WithImpulses(row,
                Impulse.FromAmount(total), row.TangentImpulse, row.BitangentImpulse)),
            world.Gravity,
            world.TimeStep,
            world.Solver);
    }

    // One position sweep over every row.
    SolvePositionPass(world: RigidWorld3D): RigidWorld3D
        => Indices(world.Constraints.Count).Reduce(world, (acc, i) => SolvePositionRow(acc, i));

    // The PSEUDO-VELOCITIES that remove the remaining overlap: the same world with
    // every body's twist reset to zero and every row's accumulator reset to zero,
    // and `PositionIterations` position sweeps run on it. The result is not a state
    // the simulation is ever in — only its `Bodies` twists are meaningful, and only
    // as a displacement rate for one step.
    SolvePositions(world: RigidWorld3D): Array<SolverBody3D>
    {
        var zero = Impulse.FromAmount(0.0);
        var atRest = RigidWorld3D(
            world.Bodies.Map(body => AtRest(body)),
            world.Constraints.Map(row => WithImpulses(row, zero, zero, zero)),
            world.Gravity,
            world.TimeStep,
            world.Solver);
        return Indices(world.TimeStep.PositionIterations)
            .Reduce(atRest, (acc, i) => SolvePositionPass(acc))
            .Bodies;
    }

    //==
    // # The step
    //
    // One fixed step, as a pure function of the world. The order is forced:
    // velocities must be final before positions move (semi-implicit Euler), and
    // contacts must be solved before that, or the step would move bodies through
    // each other and solve the interpenetration next frame.

    // The world with gravity and damping applied to every body's velocity, and no
    // other wrench. A caller with per-body forces calls `IntegrateVelocity` itself
    // with the wrench it assembled; this is the free-fall case, which is the one a
    // scene without actuators is in.
    ApplyGravityAndDamping(world: RigidWorld3D): RigidWorld3D
    {
        var seconds = world.TimeStep.FixedDeltaTime.Seconds;
        var free = SpatialForce3D(Vector3D.Zero, Vector3D.Zero);
        return RigidWorld3D(
            world.Bodies.Map(body => IntegrateVelocity(body, free, world.Gravity, seconds)),
            world.Constraints,
            world.Gravity,
            world.TimeStep,
            world.Solver);
    }

    // The world with every body's pose advanced by its velocity plus the matching
    // pseudo-velocity. `corrections` is `SolvePositions`' output and must be the
    // same length as `Bodies`.
    IntegratePoses(world: RigidWorld3D, corrections: Array<SolverBody3D>): RigidWorld3D
    {
        var seconds = world.TimeStep.FixedDeltaTime.Seconds;
        return RigidWorld3D(
            Indices(world.Bodies.Count).Map(i =>
                IntegratePoseWith(world.Bodies[i], corrections[i].Velocity, seconds)),
            world.Constraints,
            world.Gravity,
            world.TimeStep,
            world.Solver);
    }

    // ONE FIXED STEP: apply gravity and damping, solve contact velocities, work out
    // the positional correction, then move. The returned world carries the solved
    // impulses in its constraint rows, which is what the next frame's
    // `WarmStartFrom` reads.
    //
    // Contacts are NOT regenerated here. Detection needs shapes and this record
    // holds none, so the caller refreshes `Constraints` between steps — which is
    // also what lets the same step drive a scene of spheres, a scene of boxes, or a
    // scene whose contacts came from somewhere else entirely.
    Step(world: RigidWorld3D): RigidWorld3D
    {
        var solved = SolveVelocities(ApplyGravityAndDamping(world));
        return IntegratePoses(solved, SolvePositions(solved));
    }

    // `count` fixed steps. Substepping is the cheapest accuracy there is: halving
    // the step halves the integrator's error and doubles the effective stiffness of
    // every contact, at the same cost per unit of simulated time as one long step
    // with twice the iterations — and unlike more iterations it also fixes fast
    // bodies passing through thin ones.
    StepMany(world: RigidWorld3D, count: Integer): RigidWorld3D
        => Indices(count).Reduce(world, (acc, i) => Step(acc));

    // ONE FRAME of a scene made of balls and one ground plane: refresh the contacts
    // against the bodies' current poses, carrying last frame's accumulated impulses
    // across, and then step. The whole simulation loop of such a scene is repeated
    // application of this function to its own result.
    StepBallScene(world: RigidWorld3D, radii: Array<Number>, ground: Plane,
        groundBody: BodyIndex, friction: Number, restitution: Proportion,
        matchTolerance: Length): RigidWorld3D
        => Step(RigidWorld3D(
            world.Bodies,
            BallSceneConstraints(world, radii, ground, groundBody, friction, restitution,
                matchTolerance),
            world.Gravity,
            world.TimeStep,
            world.Solver));

    //==
    // # Settings and materials worth starting from
    //
    // Named values, not defaults: nothing here is applied unless a caller asks for
    // it. They exist so that a first scene is a few lines rather than a search for
    // plausible numbers, and so that the numbers a reader sees in a demo have a
    // name saying what they are.

    // Uniform gravity at the Earth's surface, pointing down the world -Z axis.
    // Convention: see CONVENTIONS.md - World space
    Earth(_: UniformGravity3D): UniformGravity3D
        => UniformGravity3D(Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, -9.80665));

    // A sixty-hertz fixed step with the iteration counts a real-time simulation
    // usually settles on: velocity iterations dominate contact stiffness and
    // position iterations only remove leftover overlap, so the first number is the
    // larger. MaxStepsPerFrame bounds catch-up after a long frame, which is what
    // stops a stalled tab from simulating a minute of physics on resume.
    SixtyHertz(_: TimeStepSettings): TimeStepSettings
        => TimeStepSettings(Duration(1.0 / 60.0), 1, 8, 3, 4);
```
